item.title: Ranking and Unranking Permutations in Heap's Order
item.description: arXiv:2611.05397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heap's algorithm is a permutation generation method with very low constant overhead. Its element-interchanging mechanism, however, prevents the standard factorial-base Lehmer code from being applied directly, and to our knowledge no explicit Rank/Unrank algorithm for the Heap order has been published. This paper describes the block structure of Heap's algorithm in terms of rearrangement operators: the net effect of a block-internal traversal is a tail-preserving operator and the block-boundary swap is a top-level swap operator, and together they yield a closed-form recurrence for the block transitions. On this basis a bottom-up Unrank algorithm and a top-down Rank algorithm are built from one and the same closed-form in-block mapping; both run in $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n)$ space and require no factorial-scale precomputed table. The supporting proofs use a synchronized strong induction on the dimension to establish the bijectivity of the trailing-element mapping, closed forms for the final arrangement and for the trailing sequence, the dichotomy of its cycle structure, and the reciprocity of Rank and Unrank. The Heap order is in fact the colex order of the mixed-radix code.
item.dc:creator: Yusheng Hu

item.title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.05446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Montanari's incremental approximate message passing (IAMP) algorithm [FOCS 2019; SIAM J. Comput., 2025] and the zero-temperature formulation of El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke (AMS) [Ann. Probab., 2021] find a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation to the maximum Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) energy in $C(\varepsilon)N^2$ operations for fixed accuracy, with probability tending to one as $N\to\infty$, under their respective full-support and access-model assumptions. However, it was unknown whether this approximation could be achieved with work polynomial in both $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$, together with quantitative guarantees at finite dimension. Under the same assumptions as AMS, we introduce grouped IAMP with exact Gaussian query outputs (GEG-IAMP), which is the first SK approximation algorithm with total work polynomial in $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and a finite-size guarantee above a dimension threshold polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ and $\log(1/\alpha)$. More precisely, for every $\alpha\in(0,1/2)$, it returns a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation with probability at least $1-\alpha$ whenever $N\ge \mathsf{K}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(e/\varepsilon)\log(\mathsf{K}/\alpha)$, using $O(N^2/\varepsilon)$ work and $O(N^2)$ storage. GEG-IAMP replaces the Onsager correction by Reeves's coupling construction [arXiv:2508.10782] and groups Euler-Maruyama steps into $O(1/\varepsilon)$ matrix-vector products. We also prove a relative guarantee for AMS IAMP with $O(N^2\varepsilon^{-3}\log^2(e/\varepsilon))$ work but a sufficient dimension exponential in inverse accuracy. By returning a fixed configuration below its dimension threshold, GEG-IAMP also provides an asymptotic fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (AFPRAS), with an additive error independent of dimension.
item.dc:creator: Dylan Herman, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Guneykan Ozgul

item.title: Improved lower bounds on the approximability of Multiway Cut using Sherali-Adams relaxations
item.description: arXiv:2611.05511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Multiway Cut problem is among the most well-studied problems in the area of combinatorial approximation algorithms. The currently best approximation ratio for the problem is 1.2787, obtained recently by the authors (2026). The best lower bound on the approximation ratio that can be achieved for the problem in polynomial time, under the Unique Games Conjecture (UGC), is 1.20016, obtained by B\'erczi, Chandrasekaran, Kir\'aly, and Madan (2020), building on and slightly improving a bound of $\frac65=1.2$, obtained by Angelidakis, Makarychev, and Manurangsi (2017) by introducing the important framework of non-opposite multiway cuts. We obtain a substantially improved lower bound of 1.22232 on the approximation ratio of the Multiway Cut problem. Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz (2008) showed that under UGC, the approximation ratio of Multiway Cut is equal to the integrality ratio of a simple LP relaxation, known as the CKR relaxation, introduced by C\u{a}linescu, Karloff, and Rabani (2000). Thus, stronger LP relaxations are not required for obtaining an optimal approximation algorithm for the problem. We show, however, that relying on the framework of Angelidakis, Makarychev, and Manurangsi (2017), stronger LP relaxations from the Sherali-Adams hierarchy for non-opposite multiway cuts can be used to obtain improved integrality ratios for the CKR relaxation, and hence improved lower bounds on the approximation ratio of the Multiway Cut problem. One of the novel features of our analysis is considering a continuous limit of discrete LPs defined on a simplex. Our proof of the new 1.22232 bound is completely analytic. We also present strong numerical evidence that suggests that our techniques can be used to improve the lower bound to at least 1.23003.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Brakensiek, Neng Huang, Aaron Potechin, Uri Zwick

item.title: Fast Quantum Byzantine Agreement with Nearly Linear Quantum Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.05598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider synchronous binary Byzantine agreement among $n$ processes connected by authenticated point-to-point classical and quantum channels. The adversary is computationally unbounded, sees all classical information, adaptively corrupts up to $t\le(1/3-\varepsilon)n$ processes, and may suppress messages sent by a process in the round in which it is corrupted. We give a quantum algorithm that solves Byzantine agreement in this model with probability $1$. It uses $O(\log^4 n)$ rounds, $O(n\log^8 n)$ qubits, and $O(n^2\log^8 n)$ classical bits in expectation, with constants depending on $\varepsilon$. This reduces the quantum communication of the protocol of Ben-Or and Hassidim (STOC~2005), which achieves $O(1)$ expected rounds but whose Byzantine coin implementation requires $\Omega(n^4\log n)$ qubits and classical bits. We also extend the quadratic message lower bound of Abraham et al.\ (PODC~2019) to quantum channels, obtaining an $\Omega(t^2)$ lower bound on worst-case expected total communication. For $t=\Theta(n)$, the communication and round complexity of our algorithm are therefore optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.
item.dc:creator: Jan Olkowski

item.title: Private Online Release of Adaptive Linear Queries
item.description: arXiv:2611.05602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we study answering counting and other linear queries online under differential privacy constraints. Recent work by Nikolov, Tang, and Ullman [STOC 2026] gave the first online algorithm that answers \emph{obliviously chosen} online linear queries privately, and achieves poly-logarithmic competitiveness against an optimal offline factorization mechanism. This also implied poly-logarithmic competitiveness against arbitrary private offline mechanisms when the private dataset is large enough. The error guarantees of their algorithm, however, can fail when the queries are adaptive. We give a new algorithm that also achieves poly-logarithmic competitiveness, while being able to handle \emph{adaptively chosen} queries. This implies that there is no large separation between the optimal error bounds for privately answering, respectively, offline linear queries, obliviously chosen online linear queries, and adaptively chosen online linear queries. Our algorithm combines the online factorization approach from prior work with a novel layered Euclidean iterative database construction, presenting a new way to use factorization in private algorithms. We also give a lower bound that shows that some poly-logarithmic factor in the competitive ratio is unavoidable. Our lower bound first shows that any interactive private mechanism implies a deterministic online factorization algorithm, and then gives a new lower bound for the competitive ratio of any deterministic online factorization algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Aleksandar Nikolov, Haohua Tang

item.title: The Harmonic Online $k$-Server Algorithm Is Poly(k)-Competitive
item.description: arXiv:2611.05669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The online $k$-server problem is one of the most fundamental problems in online algorithms. In this problem, $k$ servers are located in a metric space and serve a sequence of requests at points in the metric space by moving a server there. The Harmonic algorithm is a very natural algorithm: it chooses a server with probability inversely proportional to its distance from the request. It is also highly efficient, being memoryless and answering each request in $O(k)$ time. However, its competitive ratio has remained unsettled between the $O(2^k \log k)$ upper bound (Bartal and Grove, JACM 2000) and the $k(k+1)/2$ lower bound (Raghavan and Snir, 1994, IBM J. Res. Dev.). We prove that Harmonic is $2k^4$-competitive on every metric space against adaptive online adversaries. Our analysis uses a potential combining corrected electrical energy with the distances of online servers to their assigned adversary locations.
item.dc:creator: Yichen Huang

item.title: Reachability Diameter: Beyond the Square-Root Barrier, with Polynomial Hardness
item.description: arXiv:2611.05712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The reachability diameter of a directed graph is the maximum finite shortest-path distance across all pairs of vertices. It has received recent attention under this name, although the underlying quantity has long played a central role in shortcut set and parallel reachability. Notably, Bals et al. establish hardness for every polynomial-factor approximation in nearly-linear time for weighted digraphs. Yet they give $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in the unweighted regime with nearly-linear running time, and their conditional lower bounds rule out certain constants only, leaving open whether polynomial loss is necessary. We give a randomized algorithm that estimates the reachability diameter of an unweighted digraph within a factor $n^{1/3+o(1)}$, with high probability, in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time. We complement our algorithm with a lower bound conditional on the 3-uniform Hyperclique hypothesis, ruling out an $n^{2/15-\varepsilon}$-approximation in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2/15)$, establishing the necessity of polynomial loss for nearly-linear time algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Hector Tierno, Shuang Yang

item.title: Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees on a Napkin
item.description: arXiv:2611.05713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the incremental minimum spanning forest problem, weighted edges arrive one at a time. After each insertion we must report the edge that leaves the minimum spanning forest, and queries ask for the bottleneck distance of two vertices: the smallest possible maximum edge cost on a path between them. Link-cut trees solve both in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. In 2021 we wrote the folklore BottleneckTree, a short competitive-programming structure that stores one parent pointer and one cost per vertex, and conjectured that it also runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. We show that this conjecture is false: on a family of inputs, its amortized cost per operation is $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. We then present a structure with the same state, two arrays and a single loop, and prove that it runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time per insertion and per query. Unlike the AM-tree of Ding, Gu and Sun, which attains the same bound, it stores no subtree sizes and maintains no balance invariant. For a connected graph with distinct costs, the structure can be viewed as an implicit link-cut tree on the Kruskal reconstruction tree: each rotation corresponds to exactly one preferred-child change, and each skip acts on a stale path-parent pointer. In experiments it is 1.3-2.1 times faster than the folklore BottleneckTree on insertions, up to 480 times faster on its adversarial input, and 6.3-16 times faster than an explicit link-cut tree.
item.dc:creator: Lucian Bicsi, Adrian Bud\u{a}u

item.title: Faster Approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances via Near-Optimal Sumset Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.05725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: \emph{Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances} is one of the most studied problems in string algorithms: given a text $T$ of length~$n$ and a pattern~$P$, the task is to compute the Hamming distance between~$P$ and every length-$|P|$ substring of~$T$. As exact algorithms have been stuck at time~$\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ for decades, a long line of work has turned to the $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate version of the problem. Milestones include Karloff's $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2} n)$-time algorithm [IPL '93], followed by randomized improvements to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-1} n)$ by Kopelowitz and Porat [FOCS '15] and recently to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-0.915} n)$ by Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu [FOCS '23]. In this work, we significantly improve this bound to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2/3} n)$, using a considerably simpler algorithm. Our algorithm follows the framework of Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu, which reduces the problem to a variant of 3SUM that we call \emph{Sumset Estimation}. We solve Sumset Estimation optimally (up to logarithmic factors) by replacing their matrix multiplication techniques with ideas from sparse recovery. Specifically, we adapt the classic Count Sketch by replacing its random signs with random complex roots of unity---a simple idea that may find further applications for other additive problems. Finally, we give evidence that our running time might in fact be optimal: we show that the $\epsilon^{-2/3}$ dependence is \emph{best possible} for a certain natural class of algorithms, including ours and all previous algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Nick Fischer, Yael Kirkpatrick, Vasileios Nakos

item.title: Flow-Optimal Separators for Minor-Free and Induced-Minor-Free Graphs in Linear Time via Follow the Regularized Leader
item.description: arXiv:2611.05756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a new algorithm for finding balanced separators in minor-free and induced-minor-free graphs. A key technical idea is a new connection to online learning: we formulate a continuous, non-convex optimization problem and solve it using the Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) framework. Our implementation of each FTRL step yields a purely combinatorial algorithm that assigns and adjusts vertex weights over multiple rounds. For graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, we obtain the following results. (1) For $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(\log(|V(H)|)\sqrt{|V(H)|+|E(H)|}\sqrt{m})$ in expected linear time for fixed $H$. As a corollary, we find balanced separators of size $O(\sqrt{m})$ in string graphs in expected linear time, without requiring string representations. (2) For $K_h$-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(h\log h\sqrt{n})$ in expected linear time for fixed $h$. Our algorithm unifies two long lines of work on separators in minor-free graphs, dating back to Alon, Seymour, and Thomas (1990): one optimizing separator size and the other optimizing running time. It also gives a natural interpretation of the vertex weighting scheme in a recent linear-time algorithm by Bonnet, Korhonen, Le, Li, and Masarik (2026). The separator bounds for both graph classes are flow-optimal: techniques based on flow-cut duality, including ours, cannot yield balanced separators of asymptotically smaller size.
item.dc:creator: Hung Le, Jack Spalding-Jamieson

item.title: Noncrossing is All You Need: Beyond Identical Delay Functions in Online Matching with Delays on General Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2611.05769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online optimization with delays has emerged as a powerful paradigm with numerous applica- tions, including matching, caching, server management, network design, and set cover. In most of these problems, competitive algorithms are known for arbitrary monotone delay functions, even when different requests are associated with different delay functions. The notable exception is online matching with delays, where all previously known algorithms achieving constant or polylogarithmic competitive ratios require the delay functions to be identical, either linear or concave, and known in advance. We study the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delays problem on general metrics. We introduce the broad class of noncrossing delay functions, which strictly generalizes the classic setting of identical concave delay functions while naturally modeling scenarios in which different requests may experience different delay costs. We present the first deterministic $O(1)$-competitive algorithm for the single-location online matching problem with noncrossing delay functions in the non-clairvoyant setting as well as a randomized $O(lognlog\Delta+log^2\Delta)$-competitive algorithm of an arbitrary metric space where $n$ is the number of points of the metric space and $\Delta$ is its aspect ratio. Our result allows each request to have an arbitrary noncrossing delay function, thereby simultaneously removing the assumptions of identical delay functions, concavity, and clairvoyance that were required by all previous constant or polylogarithmic-competitive algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Yossi Azar, Junhao Gan, Shahar Lewkowicz, Xiao Sun, Seeun William Umboh

item.title: Makespan Bounds for Synchronous Pebble Motion on Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.05839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the largest minimum makespan of labeled pebble motion on graphs under a model that permits synchronous pebble movement. While classical pebble motion on graphs allows only one pebble to move at a time, our model permits any number of pebbles to move to an adjacent vertex, provided that no two pebbles collide. At full occupancy every vertex is assigned a pebble and a legal round consists of disjoint cycle rotations. We prove a series of makespan bounds for this problem on graphs with varying structure and pebble density. For cycles with a chord, we extend a known quadratic bound at span two to every fixed span. For random cubic graphs, we convert permutation routing via matchings into legal schedules in two ways, applying cycle-cover batching at full occupancy and disjoint vacancy-delivery paths below full occupancy. For simple 3-connected planar cubic graphs, we prove a tight linear class maximum at every pebble count. We extend the results to increasing degree, common-neighbor conditions, and vertex connectivity. The results describe how graph connectivity, cycle structure, expansion, planarity, and occupancy affect worst-case routing time.
item.dc:creator: Lucy McManamon, Jingjin Yu

item.title: Improved Bounds on Distance Preservers
item.description: arXiv:2611.05878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given an undirected unweighted graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and a set $P$ of $p$ pairs of its vertices, a distance preserver is a sparse subgraph of $G$ that exactly preserves the shortest-path distances between all pairs in $P$. In this paper, we prove a new upper bound of $O(n^{8/9} p^{4/9})$ for distance preservers when $p\in [n^{1/2}, n]$. Our result improves the previous bound of $O\big(n^{2/3}p^{2/3}+np^{1/3}\big)$ by Bodwin and Vassilevska Williams and $O(\min\{n+n^{1/2}p,\,np^{1/2}\})$ by Coppersmith and Elkin, particularly in the regime $p\in [n^{7/10}, n]$, and narrows the gap toward the conjectured $O(n^{2/3}p^{2/3}+n)$ bound. Using the techniques developed for distance preservers, we are also able to obtain pairwise additive $+2$ spanners with $O(n+n^{9/10}p^{2/5})$ edges, pairwise additive $+4$ spanners with $O(n+n^{24/25}p^{8/25})$ edges, and new bounds for sourcewise spanners, improving upon previous results in certain parameter regimes.
item.dc:creator: Yanyu Chen, Yu Chen, Zihan Tan, Mingyang Yang

item.title: Improved approximation algorithms for capacitated cluster editing
item.description: arXiv:2611.05916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimum-disagreement cluster editing problem that, from a complete edge-signed graph, where a positive edge represents two vertices agreeing to each other while a negative represents a disagreement, constructs disjoint cliques of upper bounded size such that the total number of negative edges inside cliques and positive edges outside cliques is minimized. When the sizes of the candidate cliques are unbounded, the problem is NP-hard and APX-hard, and many approximation algorithms with improving ratios have been proposed in the literature and the state-of-the-art approximation ratio of $\alpha = 1.3865 + \epsilon$. The capacitated variant, in which the candidate cliques have sizes no greater than a given $k$, is less studied and the best approximation ratio is $5.37$. In this paper, we study the latter problem. We first present a downsizing procedure that achieves an approximation ratio of $\alpha_k = 2 \alpha + 1$, based on any $\alpha$-approximation algorithm for the uncapacitated problem. Secondly, we propose a hybrid of cluster-LP sampling and pivoting and show that for every fractional capacitated cluster-LP solution of cost $L$, the hybrid using ordinary pivoting has an expected cost at most $\frac 95 L + \frac 1{10} \OPT_k$, and the hybrid using conditional pivoting has an expected cost at most $\frac {306}{203} L + \frac {50}{203} \OPT_k$. A cardinality-constrained adaptation of the approximate dual-separation framework of Garc\'ia-Soriano and Schohn supplies the required fractional solution and yields a randomized $(1.9 + \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm and a randomized $(1.7537 + \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Cong Ma, Guangting Chen, Yong Chen, Guohui Lin, Jiaxuan Ma, Lusheng Wang

item.title: Faster Isomorphism for Groups of Class 2
item.description: arXiv:2611.05920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The finite-group isomorphism problem asks whether two groups, given by their Cayley tables, are isomorphic. Despite decades of study, obtaining an $N^{o(\log N)}$-time algorithm for general groups of order $N$ remains a major open challenge. Groups of nilpotency class $2$ have long been a central obstacle to achieving this goal. Recent breakthroughs have established $N^{o(\log N)}$-time algorithms for $p$-groups of class $2$ with odd $p$ (Sun, STOC '23; Ivanyos-Mendoza-Qiao-Sun-Zhang, FOCS '24; Grochow-Qiao-Stange-Sun, STOC '25) and for groups of Frattini class $2$ (Grochow-Ivanyos-Qiao-Sun, FOCS '26). However, the problem remained open for general groups of class $2$. In this paper, we present an algorithm for testing isomorphism of groups of class $2$, with running time $N^{O((\log N)^{25/26} \log \log N)}$. Our algorithm combines a tensor-based restriction of the search space, an encoding of group relations by alternating matrix tuples, and an orbit computation to recover the remaining central power information.
item.dc:creator: Xiaorui Sun

item.title: Faster Dynamic Maximal Independent Set against Adaptive Adversaries
item.description: arXiv:2611.05932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fully dynamic maximal independent set (MIS) problem: maintaining an MIS in an undirected graph on $n$ vertices with at most $m$ edges under edge insertions and deletions. Against an oblivious adversary, which fixes the edge update sequence in advance, the randomized algorithms of Behnezhad et al. (2019) and Chechik and Zhang (2019) achieve polylogarithmic update time. Against an adaptive adversary, which may choose each update after observing the previously reported MISs, the best previously known update bound was $O(m^{2/3})$, given by the deterministic algorithm of Gupta and Khan (2018, 2021). Assuming the combinatorial Boolean matrix multiplication hypothesis, Bernstein et al. (2026) proved that any combinatorial algorithm against an adaptive adversary requires at least $m^{1/2-o(1)}$ update time even under edge insertions alone, leaving a polynomial gap between upper and lower bounds. We present a randomized fully dynamic MIS algorithm with $\widetilde O(m^{5/8})=\widetilde O(m^{2/3-1/24})$ update time against adaptive adversaries. This gives the first polynomial improvement over the $m^{2/3}$ bound for adaptive fully dynamic MIS.
item.dc:creator: Hongyi Chen, Shuyan Fan, Tianyi Zhang

item.title: Single-Variable Connectivity in Random $k$-SAT
item.description: arXiv:2611.05981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We resolve longstanding questions about connectivity, reconstruction,and looseness in random $k$-SAT, for sufficiently large fixed $k$ as the number $n$ of variables tends to infinity. $\textbf{Single-variable connectivity up to reconstruction.}$ At clause densities up to \[\frac{2^k}{k}\bigl(\ln k+\ln\ln k+\gamma_*-o_k(1)\bigr),\] a polynomial-time algorithm joins a typical pair of satisfying assignments with high probability, using $O_k(n)$ single-variable flips that preserve satisfiability. Here $\gamma_*\approx0.871$ arises from a refined tree-reconstruction analysis. $\textbf{Settling the reconstruction threshold.}$ Building on the tools developed for connectivity, we determine the clustering threshold defined by the reconstruction criterion to be \[\frac{2^k}{k}\bigl(\ln k+\ln\ln k+\gamma_*+o_k(1)\bigr),\] below the classical cavity prediction with constant term $1+O(\ln\ln k/\ln k)$. $\textbf{Shattering before rigidity.}$ We locate the looseness--rigidity transition at a higher density, matching the classical cavity prediction for clustering: \[\frac{2^k}{k} \left(\ln k+\ln\ln k+1+\Theta\left(\frac{\ln\ln k}{\ln k}\right)\right).\] Below the transition, we establish a stronger form of looseness: any variable of a typical solution can be reversed by logarithmically many single-variable flips that preserve satisfiability. Above it, reversing most variables of a typical solution requires changing linearly many variables (rigidity). Yet throughout an interval between reconstruction and rigidity, the solution space already splits into groups of exponentially small relative size separated by linear Hamming distance and linear energy barriers (shattering), while logarithmic looseness persists.
item.dc:creator: Chunyang Wang, Yitong Yin, Yixiao Yu, Yiyao Zhang

item.title: Single-Exponential FPT Algorithms for Minimum Bisection and Matching Cut via a New Unbreakable Decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2611.05982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimum Bisection asks whether the vertices of a graph can be partitioned into two parts whose sizes differ by at most one and with at most k edges between the two parts. Cygan, Lokshtanov, Marcin Pilipczuk, Micha{\l} Pilipczuk, and Saurabh (SICOMP 2019) gave the first fixed-parameter algorithm, which runs in O*(2^(O(k^3))) time, by introducing an unbreakable decomposition. Cygan, Komosa, Lokshtanov, Marcin Pilipczuk, Micha{\l} Pilipczuk, Saurabh, and Wahlstr\"om (TALG 2021) strengthened the decomposition and improved the running time to O*(2^(O(k log k))). However, whether the running time could be improved to single-exponential remained open. In this paper, we give a deterministic O*(2^(O(k)))-time algorithm for Minimum Bisection. Our algorithm also counts all feasible bisections. To obtain an O*(2^(O(k)))-time algorithm, we introduce two new techniques. First, we give a new algorithm that computes a (2k,k)-edge-unbreakable decomposition with adhesion at most 2k in O*(2^(O(k))) time by relaxing the unbreakability and adhesion guarantees of the decomposition in (TALG 2021). Second, we improve the running time of the dynamic program over the decomposition from O*(2^(O(k log k))) to O*(2^(O(k))) using important cuts, inclusion-exclusion, and formal logarithms and exponentials. Together with color coding, the same techniques give a deterministic O*(2^(O(k)))-time algorithm for Matching Cut, which asks for a cut whose crossing edges form a matching. This improves the O*(2^(O(k log k)))-time algorithm of Aravind and Saxena (IWOCA 2021).
item.dc:creator: Soh Kumabe

item.title: Faster Cluster Decomposition with Stronger Bi-Criteria Guarantee
item.description: arXiv:2611.06008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partitioning the vertex set of a graph $G=(V,E)$ into clusters is a classical problem in computer science. As vertices within clusters should be well connected and cuts between clusters sparse, Oveis Gharan and Trevisan (SODA 2014, [OGT14]) proposed to measure the partition quality using inner and outer conductance, i.e., the bi-criteria guarantee. Specifically, when partitioning $V$ into vertex-disjoint subsets $P_1,\ldots, P_k$, every subgraph induced by $P_i$ should have high conductance, while the conductance of $P_i$ in $G$ should be low. They studied the existence of such a partition and designed a polynomial-time algorithm achieving this guarantee. For more than a decade, their algorithm remained the only one achieving this guarantee on its output clusters. In this paper, we study faster cluster decomposition algorithms under the same setup as [OGT14] and prove three results: 1. We make their existential result algorithmic: Our algorithms run in nearly-linear time, and achieve the same bi-criteria guarantee as the one in [OGT14] up to constant factors, including the asymptotically tight dependence on $k$. 2. We prove that their existential result holds algorithmically under a much weaker condition on the initial disjoint subsets. To achieve this, we develop a general algorithm framework that boosts the approximation guarantee of a solution: given an $\alpha$-approximate solution to the $k$-way conductance problem, if $\rho_G(k+1)/\rho_G(k)=\Omega\left(\alpha/\varepsilon\right)$, then a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution can be obtained using only $O(k(1+\log\alpha))$ minimum $s$-$t$ cut computations. 3. We present a nearly-linear time algorithm that finds clusters with the bi-criteria guarantee. Our algorithm has the same guarantee as the one in [OGT14], which, for any unweighted graph of $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, runs in $\widetilde{O}(knm^2)$ time.
item.dc:creator: He Sun, Yong Zhang, Yacong Zhou

item.title: Optimal LCA and Sublinear Estimation for Bipartite Matching in $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ Queries
item.description: arXiv:2611.06024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A local computation algorithm (LCA) for matching answers ``who is the mate of $v$?'' by inspecting only a small part of the graph, with all answers consistent with one matching. For $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$, Levi et al. [Algorithmica'17] give a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate matching LCA using $(\Delta/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)} \operatorname{polylog}(n)$ queries per invocation, while Yoshida et al. [SIAM J. Comput.'12] estimate the maximum matching size within additive error $\varepsilon n$ using $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}$ queries. Behnezhad, Roghani, and Rubinstein [FOCS'23] proved a $\Delta^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)}$ lower bound for both tasks, even on bipartite graphs and even when the LCA's matching guarantee is relaxed to additive $\varepsilon n$ error. This leaves a gap between linear and quadratic dependence on $1/\varepsilon$ in the exponent. We close this gap on bipartite graphs. We give an LCA that answers each mate query with $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ queries for a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate matching, and an estimator for the maximum matching size within $\varepsilon n$ using $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ queries. On general graphs, the same algorithm gives a half-integral fractional matching and estimates the maximum fractional matching size. Our approach runs $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log\Delta)$ rounds of a deterministic local optimization method in which vertices propose to neighbors and update prices according to incoming loads. We design its updates to admit exact recursive sampling with constant expected branching, obtaining the improved randomized bound without exploring full dependency neighborhoods. To our knowledge, this is the first LCA construction based on exact recursive sampling of the iterates of a deterministic continuous optimization method. We expect this approach to have applications beyond matching.
item.dc:creator: Edith Cohen, Mohammad Roghani

item.title: Softmax Attention with Any Temperature in Fixed Dimension: Matching the Best Known Maximum-Inner-Product Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2611.06055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention is central to modern AI models for language, vision, and scientific modeling. However, direct evaluation compares every query with every key, requiring quadratic time in the context length, which limits its scalability to long contexts. Consequently, characterizing the complexity bounds of attention is of fundamental importance. For every fixed dimension $d$, we give an algorithm for $m$ queries, $n$ key-value pairs, and additive error $\varepsilon$, with expected time $ \widetilde{\mathrm{O}}\bigl((mn)^{k/(k+1)}+m+n\bigr),\qquad k=\lfloor d/2\rfloor. $ For fixed dimension and a fixed number of value channels, soft-O hides factors of the form $\operatorname{poly}_d\bigl(b,\log(m+n),\log B,\log(1/\varepsilon)\bigr),$ where $b$ bounds input encoding lengths and $B$ bounds coordinate and value magnitudes. In particular, the dependence on $B$ and $1/\varepsilon$ is polylogarithmic, which allows arbitrary positive temperature. When $m=n$ and $d\ge2$, the bound is $\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^{2-2/(\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1)})$: near-linear in dimensions two and three, with exponent $4/3$ in dimensions four and five and $3/2$ in dimensions six and seven. It improves the previous $\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^{2-1/d})$ upper bound and matches the best known batch maximum-inner-product bound in each fixed dimension. Additionally, we reduce integer batch maximum inner product computation to one attention call with the same dimension and input sizes $m,n$.

item.title: Constant-Round Massively Parallel Algorithms for Approximate MSTs in Metric Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.06092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a unified algorithmic framework for computing approximate minimum spanning trees (MSTs) in metric spaces in the fully scalable Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Using this framework, we obtain the following results for any fixed constant $\sigma\in(0,1)$: - General metrics: Given all pairwise distances, we compute a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate MST in $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ rounds using $n^\sigma$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ total space. - Euclidean spaces: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we compute an $O(1/\sigma^4)$-approximate MST in $O(1)$ rounds using $(nd)^\sigma$ local space per machine and $O(nd+n^{1+\sigma})$ total space. - Doubling metrics: Given $n$ points in a metric of doubling dimension $\mathrm{ddim}=O(\sigma\log n)$, we compute an $O(1/\sigma)$-approximate MST in $O(\mathrm{ddim}/\sigma^4)$ rounds using $n^\sigma$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^{1+\sigma})\cdot 2^{O(\mathrm{ddim})}$ total space. For any fixed constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, these results give the first constant-round MPC algorithms achieving $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation in general metrics and $O(1)$-approximation in a high-dimensional Euclidean space, respectively. They improve upon the $O(\log\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))$-round algorithm for general metrics [SODA'25] and the $O(\log\log n\cdot\log\log\log n)$-round algorithm for Euclidean spaces [SODA'24], respectively. Moreover, our round complexity for general metrics is asymptotically optimal in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, matching the $\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ lower bound of [SODA'25] under the 1-vs-2-cycles conjecture. Our result also answers an open question raised by [STOC'23].
item.dc:creator: Eunjin Oh, Hyeonjun Shin

item.title: Sublinear Approximations for Spanning Tree Congestion
item.description: arXiv:2611.06209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spanning tree congestion of a connected graph \(G\) is the minimum, over all spanning trees \(T\) of \(G\), of the maximum number of edges of \(G\) crossing a cut induced by deleting an edge of \(T\). In the spanning tree congestion problem we are asked to compute a spanning tree with minimum congestion. We describe two sublinear-ratio approximation algorithms for the spanning tree congestion problem (STC): a simple $\Ot(n^{8/9})$-approximation, and a more involved $\Ot(n^{2/3})$-approximation, where the notation $\Ot$ hides factors polynomial in $\log n$.. Until now, no algorithm with sublinear ratio was known. We also prove that for any fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, approximation of the spanning tree congestion within $2-\varepsilon$ is NP-hard. This improves the previous best known lower bound $6/5$.
item.dc:creator: Sunny Atalig, Marek Chrobak, Petr Kolman, Hans Raj Tiwary

item.title: Consistent Submodular Maximization with Full Foresight
item.description: arXiv:2611.06223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online algorithms with bounded recourse face three intertwined obstacles: uncertainty about the future, computational limits, and a limited budget for changes. We ask a fundamental question that separates consistency from the other two: what does solution stability cost when the entire future is known and computation is unlimited? We answer this question for monotone submodular maximization, where an algorithm must maintain a solution of at most $k$ arrived elements, with a constant number of changes per step. We determine the optimal approximation thresholds: $3/4$ for deterministic algorithms and $\xi^\star \approx 0.7942$ for randomized algorithms. For every $\varepsilon>0$, we get within $\varepsilon$ of these thresholds with worst-case recourse polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$, independent of $k$ and the stream length. We prove matching impossibility results even for coverage functions. We attain the sharp bounds by optimally balancing two opposing forces: preparing for future arrivals and protecting the current solution. For randomized algorithms, we use addition robustness against prefixes of the known future, which we analyze tightly via an interval-selection problem. For deterministic algorithms, we introduce certificates, paths in a fractional relaxation that maintain high value, which we round into an update schedule.
item.dc:creator: Eric Balkanski, Paul D\"utting, Federico Fusco, Silvio Lattanzi, Ashkan Norouzi-Fard, Ola Svensson, Morteza Zadimoghaddam

item.title: A Dichotomy for Terminal Cyclability
item.description: arXiv:2611.06234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given an undirected graph $G$ and a set $R \subseteq V(G)$ of terminals, Terminal Cyclability asks whether $G$ contains a simple cycle visiting every vertex of $R$. We establish a complexity dichotomy for this problem on red-minor-closed classes of annotated graphs. In particular, we show that Terminal Cyclability is polynomial-time solvable on every such class excluding any annotated planar graph. The problem is NP-complete whenever the class contains all annotated planar graphs. More precisely, we give an $|G|^{2^{\mathbf{poly}(b)}}$-time algorithm, where $b$ is the bidimensionality of $(G,R)$. Our main technical contribution is the introduction of a weak irrelevant vertex rule. Rather than removing irrelevant vertices until the treewidth becomes constant, we only remove irrelevant vertices until the treewidth is logarithmic in the graph size. Such a weakening is necessary as a parameter-only treewidth threshold for an irrelevant vertex rule in this setting is known to be impossible to realise. Combined with a single-exponential algorithm for Terminal Cyclability parameterized by treewidth, this yields the polynomial-time algorithm for our dichotomy.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Bentert, Dario Cavallaro, Sebastian Wiederrecht

item.title: Estimating the Volume of a Union of Convex Bodies
item.description: arXiv:2611.06364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The \textit{Union Volume Estimation problem}, i.e. yielding an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-approximation of the volume of the union of convex bodies, is a classical problem in computational geometry and formal methods. In this paper, we first detect where and why the efficient union volume estimators with approximate sampling and PAC volume estimation oracles fail. Specifically, we show that having only TV-distance guarantees on the approximate sampler does not suffice, and demonstrate this bottleneck by constructing the sunflower families of convex bodies. In this context, we propose the concept of \textit{tail-controlled samplers} that can yield with high-probability almost-$\ell_{\infty}$ closeness. Secondly, we leverage this concept to propose a generic algorithmic framework \texttt{Alpona} that properly combines a PAC volume computation and approximate point sampling oracles with tail-controls to yield an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-estimate of the union volume for any collection of convex bodies. We show that \texttt{Alpona} needs only linear (in number of convex bodies) oracle calls to be $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-correct. Finally, we provide a tail-controlled analysis of the Hit-and-Run sampler~\citep{lovasz2006fast}. We further provide a novel geometric analysis to improve the required walk length of Hit-and-Run. We further instantiate \texttt{Alpona}'s correctness for the sparse frequency streams of convex bodies: a special case of the union volume estimation problem where no convex body intersects more than $\tau$ many other bodies.
item.dc:creator: Eeshan Banerjee, Aranya Kumar Bal, Debabrota Basu, Sourav Chakraborty, Debarshi Chanda, Uddalok Sarkar

item.title: Partially Dynamic Algorithms for Single-Source Temporal Paths
item.description: arXiv:2611.06387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present efficient partially dynamic algorithms for maintaining earliest arrival times from a fixed source in temporal digraphs with $n$ vertices. For the incremental scenario where updates are arc insertions, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the total number of arcs added to the arc-less graph. For the decremental scenario where updates are arc removals, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the number of arcs in the graph upon its initialization. We also consider earliest-arrival queries with an arbitrary departure-time threshold and develop an incremental algorithm with $O(n+\Delta_s m\log m)$ total update time, $O(\log m)$ query time, and $O(n+m)$ space, where $\Delta_s$ is the number of distinct departure times of arcs leaving the source. All of our algorithms are also capable of reporting an earliest arrival path from the source to the queried vertex $v$ in constant time per edge once the earliest arrival time at $v$ is known. We complement our positive results with conditional lower bounds based on the Online Boolean Matrix-Vector Multiplication conjecture (a.k.a. OMv conjecture). For both the incremental and the decremental scenarios, we show the non-existence of an algorithm with $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized update time and $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ amortized query time, even if the algorithm is randomized and latencies on the arcs are uniform. For arbitrary departure-time queries, we also establish an OMv-based conditional lower bound showing that our incremental algorithm is optimal up to logarithmic factors on dense temporal graphs. Thus, efficient total running time is essentially the best outcome we can get. Our conditional lower bounds hold also for the case of undirected temporal graphs.
item.dc:creator: Davide Bil\`o, Bart{\l}omiej Bosek, Jadwiga Czy\.zewska, Evangelos Kipouridis, Karol W\k{e}grzycki, Anna Zych-Pawlewicz

item.title: Polynomial $(2\alpha+\varepsilon)$- and Quadratic $4$-Approximation Algorithms for the Biased Traveling Salesman Problem in Bipartitioned Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.06410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is one of the fundamental problems in combinatorial optimization that asks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle in a complete undirected graph with $N$ vertices. For the metric TSP, where edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality, a long line of work has produced constant-factor approximation algorithms, culminating in the best-known approximation ratio $\alpha<3/2-10^{-36}$. The biased TSP (BTSP) generalizes the metric TSP to bipartitioned networks: the vertex set is partitioned into two subsets, edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality within each subset, while edges crossing the partition may violate it by a certain bias factor. This model captures heterogeneous routing scenarios in which distances are metric only locally but may be distorted across different regions or vertex types. Previously, the only known result for the BTSP was a $7/2$-approximation algorithm with running time $O(N^3)$. In this paper, we present two new approximation algorithms that significantly improve the state of the art. The first achieves an approximation ratio of $2\alpha+\varepsilon$ (strictly less than $3$) in polynomial time $N^{O(1)}$ for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, where the exponent grows at least linearly with $1/\varepsilon$. The second achieves a $4$-approximation in only $O(N^2)$ running time, reducing the previous cubic-time bound by a full polynomial factor. These advances directly support emerging networked systems---including multi-tier 6G architectures and hybrid quantum-classical networks---where cross-region transitions incur biased and non-metric overheads.
item.dc:creator: Jingyang Zhao, Trung Q. Duong, Een-Kee Hong, Hyundong Shin

item.title: Beyond Gomory-Hu: All-Pairs $\times$ All-Pairs Mincuts in $O(n)$ Space
item.description: arXiv:2611.06478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For over four decades, two classical structures have offered complementary views of mincuts. The Gomory-Hu tree encodes one $(x,y)$-mincut for every vertex pair $x,y$ in $O(n)$ space, but retains only one mincut per pair. In contrast, for a fixed pair $x,y$, the Picard-Queyranne representation admits an $O(n)$ space vertex ordering that determines whether some $(x,y)$-mincut separates any given pair $u,v$ and reports such a cut. Can these complementary guarantees hold simultaneously in $O(n)$ space? We answer affirmatively. For undirected graphs, we construct an $O(n)$ space structure encoding, for every four vertices $x,y,u,v$, an $(x,y)$-mincut separating $u,v$ whenever one exists. More precisely, given any terminal pair $x,y$, the structure recovers the Picard-Queyranne ordering in $O(n)$ time. Thereafter, separability queries take $O(1)$ time, and reporting a separating mincut $C$ takes $O(|C|)$ time. Thus, information for all $\Theta(n^4)$ choices of $x,y,u,v$ is encoded in $O(n)$ space. This is essentially the strongest information of this form that fits in $O(n)$ space: if one additionally requires the mincut to place $u$ on side of $x$ and $v$ on side of $y$, then $\Omega(n^2)$ space is necessary even for fixed $x,y$. As a consequence, we obtain an $O(n)$ space all-pairs mincut sensitivity oracle for a single edge failure in multigraphs, with optimal $O(n)$ time to report a new mincut. This resolves an open question of Baswana and Pandey [SODA'22] on achieving $o(n^2)$ space and $o(m)$ query time simultaneously. Our construction substantially generalizes the $O(n)$ space nearest-mincut-hierarchy [SODA'27], which reports only the nearest $(x,y)$-mincut. Recovering the entire Picard-Queyranne ordering for an arbitrary pair requires new structural properties of the Dinitz-Vainshtein [STOC'94] connectivity carcass, extending its use beyond the Steiner mincuts it represents.
item.dc:creator: Koustav Bhanja, Merav Parter, Asaf Petruschka

item.title: Computing Forest Degree Realizations with Minimum Cardinality Domination
item.description: arXiv:2611.06482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the Degree Realization problem with respect to a family $\mathcal{P}$ of graphs the input is a non-increasing sequence $d = (d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ of positive integers, and the goal is to decide whether there exists a simple undirected graph $G \in \mathcal{P}$, whose degrees correspond to $d$, i.e., such that $deg(G) = d$. In this paper we consider the version of Degree Realization in which the realization is required to be a forest (i.e., $\mathcal{P}$ is the family of forests). We consider \emph{optimized} Degree Realization in which the goal is to obtain a realization that minimizes an objective function $f$. That is, the goal is to find a realization $G$ that minimizes $f(G)$ among the realizations of the given input sequence. More specifically, we focus on the following functions: the size of an optimal \emph{vertex cover} and the size of an optimal \emph{dominating set}. We also consider the \emph{total} and \emph{paired} versions of both Min Vertex Cover and Min Dominating Set. We provide characterizations and linear time realization algorithms for all the above-mentioned problems. Since Min Paired Vertex Cover is closely related to Min Edge Dominating Set, our results for Degree Realization with respect to the former extend to the latter.
item.dc:creator: Amotz Bar-Noy, Omri Kosary, David Peleg, Dror Rawitz

item.title: A $2.81^n$ upper bound on the number of stable matchings
item.description: arXiv:2611.06494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the maximum number ${\rm SM}(n)$ of stable matchings in an instance with $n$ men and $n$ women. Karlin, Oveis Gharan, and Weber (STOC 2018) proved the first single-exponential upper bound; their argument gives ${\rm SM}(n)\le 2^{17n}$ for sufficiently large $n$. Palmer and P\'alv\"olgyi (FOCS 2021) improved this bound to $3.55^n+O(1)$. We prove that ${\rm SM}(n)<2.81^n$. This brings the exponential base closer to $2.28$, the base of the best known lower bound. More precisely, we bound the number of stable matchings in each instance in terms of each person's number of stable partners, where a stable partner is someone matched to that person in at least one stable matching. Our proof assigns each person a weight determined by this number and uses these weights to bound the number of stable matchings by induction.
item.dc:creator: Ebrahim Ghorbani, Matthias Mnich

item.title: A Sub-$3^n$ Upper Bound on the Number of Stable Matchings
item.description: arXiv:2611.06604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of determining the maximum number of stable matchings. This classical counting problem was posed by Knuth and has been studied for five decades. We obtain a new $2.999^n$ upper bound on the number of stable matchings with $n$ men and $n$ women. This improves the best-known previous result by Palmer and P\'alv\"olgyi. This result gets much closer to the well-known lower bound $\frac{2.28^n}{\text{poly}(n)}$. We refine their entropy-based framework by capturing broader structural relationships among stable matchings. To capture these relationships, we introduce new frameworks, including cones and supports. This establishes the $3.332^n$ bound. We also exploit relationships among local structures and use a charging argument to improve the bound to $2.999^n$.
item.dc:creator: Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Hikaru Wada, Masataka Yoneda

item.title: Constant-Time Dynamic Edge Coloring via Dynamic Splitting and LLL
item.description: arXiv:2611.06611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a dynamic algorithm that maintains a near-optimal edge coloring in constant expected time per update. For every fixed $\epsilon>0$, the algorithm maintains a $(1+\epsilon)\Delta$ edge coloring under edge insertions and deletions in $\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)$ worst-case expected update time against an oblivious adversary, provided $\Delta\ge\Delta_\epsilon=\widetilde\Theta(1/\epsilon^2)$. The previous constant-time algorithm of Bhattacharya, Costa, Panski, and Solomon (BCPS) required $\Delta\ge(\log n/\epsilon^4)^{\Theta(\log(1/\epsilon)/\epsilon)}$, where $n$ is the number of vertices. We remove this dependence on $n$, answering their open question. Our approach differs substantially from that of BCPS, which relied on coloring in locally tree-like subgraphs. Instead, we draw on distributed algorithms that organize partial coloring through successive applications of the Lov\'asz Local Lemma (LLL). We develop a dynamic LLL solver with worst-case expected update bounds and a dynamic splitting algorithm that partitions edges into low-degree subgraphs. A key technical contribution is a bottom-up method for iterative splitting, which avoids the logarithmic overhead of maintaining successive levels. It achieves constant expected update time by adaptively choosing which levels to inspect and repair, rather than inspecting every level after each update. We believe these dynamic splitting and LLL tools can be of interest beyond edge coloring.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Ghaffari, Sijin Peng

item.title: Deterministic Connectivity Sketches Under Edge Deletions
item.description: arXiv:2611.06626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much information about a graph is needed to determine its connectivity after arbitrary valid edge deletions? This question is at the heart of designing deterministic dynamic streaming algorithms for graph connectivity. Towards answering this question, we study the deterministic one-way communication problem in which Alice holds a graph $G_A = (V, E_A)$ on $n$ vertices, Bob holds a graph $G_B = (V, E_B)$ with $E_B \subseteq E_A$, and Alice sends a message $M \in \{0,1\}^m$ that allows Bob to decide whether $G_A - G_B$ is connected. Randomized sketches solve this problem using $\tilde O(n)$ bits, whereas deterministic recovery of even one surviving edge requires $\Omega(n^2)$ bits. We prove an upper bound of $m = \widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})$ bits and a lower bound of $m = \widetilde{\Omega}(n^{3/2})$ bits for deciding connectivity. Thus, connectivity admits a subquadratic deterministic representation despite the quadratic cost of edge recovery, but remains polynomially harder than its randomized counterpart. The upper bound immediately yields an $\widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})$-bit deterministic $n^2$-fault tolerant connectivity oracle, which reports the connected components of a graph $G$ after any valid set of edge deletions. We also obtain an $\tilde \Omega(n f^{1/4})$-bit lower bound for deterministic $f$-fault tolerant connectivity oracles for every $f \in [1,n^2]$. Finally, we show that the separation between connectivity and edge recovery persists in deterministic single-pass dynamic streams with bounded update multiplicity. For every fixed $\epsilon \in (0,1/3)$, our algorithm reports the connected components of the final simple graph using $\widetilde{O}(n^{15/8 + 3\epsilon/8})$ bits (subquadratic space), provided each edge undergoes at most $n^{\epsilon}$ insertion or deletion updates in total.
item.dc:creator: Sanjeev Khanna, Aaron Putterman, Madhu Sudan

item.title: Approximating #BIS in $\exp(\widetilde O(n^{1/3}))$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.06657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give randomized algorithms for approximately counting and nearly uniformly sampling independent sets in arbitrary bipartite graphs (#BIS). At fixed accuracy, both algorithms run in $\exp(O(n^{1/3}\log^{4/3}n))$ time on $n$-vertex graphs. More generally, the same running-time dependence on the number of variables holds for approximate counting and sampling with efficiently evaluable positive log-supermodular weights on Boolean variables. A weighted Sinclair-Jerrum walk on the self-reduction tree reduces these tasks to coarse lower estimates of residual log-partition functions. We obtain these estimates by optimizing a concave relaxation of an exact variational principle on the tree; threshold smoothing certifies that the low-degree search suffices.
item.dc:creator: Jingcheng Liu, Yitong Yin

item.title: Polynomial-Time Differentially Private Synthetic Graph Release with Nearly-Linear Additive Error
item.description: arXiv:2611.06670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a polynomial-time $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-edge-differentially private algorithm that releases a synthetic graph approximately preserving all cut values of a nonnegative weighted input graph $G$. Our algorithm outputs a nonnegative weighted graph $H$ such that, with probability at least $1-\beta$, simultaneously for all $S\subseteq V$, \[ \left|w_G(S,V\setminus S)-w_H(S,V\setminus S)\right| \leq \gamma w_G(S,V\setminus S) + O\left(\frac{n}{\gamma\varepsilon} \log^7 \frac{n}{\delta\beta\gamma\varepsilon}\right). \] For fixed $\gamma, \varepsilon$ and $\delta = \beta = n^{-10}$, the additive error is $n \operatorname{polylog} n$, improving upon the previous efficient bound of $n^{13/12 + o(1)}$. Furthermore, we establish an $\Omega(n/\gamma\varepsilon)$ lower bound for the relevant parameter regime, showing that our result is tight up to polylogarithmic factors. Our algorithm uses a log-det-regularized SDP to generate fractional queries for multiplicative-weights updates and certify accuracy for all cuts. The privacy analysis charges privacy loss only fractionally per mechanism call, based on the amount of mass on edge coordinates retired from subsequent iterations. Our synthetic graph release yields improved error bounds for several downstream tasks in private graph analysis including correlation clustering, Max-Cut, Max-$k$-Cut, constrained cut problems and hierarchical clustering. Most notably, for unweighted complete-graph correlation clustering, we achieve the optimal $\widetilde O(n)$ additive error while reducing the best previously known approximation ratio for this additive error from several thousand to $1.387$. We also provide a formalization of our results in Lean.
item.dc:creator: Marek Eli\'a\v{s}, Gautam Kamath, Janardhan Kulkarni, George Z. Li, Jingcheng Liu, Sepideh Mahabadi, Pan Peng, Jakub Tarnawski, Hangyu Xu, Zongrui Zou

item.title: The Online $k$-Taxi Problem Is Competitive on All Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2611.06684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The online $k$-taxi problem is a natural generalization of the $k$-server problem: $k$ taxis must serve a sequence of requests in a metric space. Each request is a pair of points $(r,s)$, and the algorithm serves the request by first moving a taxi to $r$ (to pick up a passenger) and then to $s$ (to drop off the passenger). The cost is the total distance traveled by the taxis without a passenger. Previous bounds for general $k$ all depended on the number of points $n$ or the aspect ratio $\Delta$ of the metric space, both of which can be infinite on general metrics, and competitive algorithms were previously known on general metrics only for $k \le 3$. In this work, we give a $9^{k-1}$-competitive randomized algorithm against adaptive online adversaries and, as a corollary, an $81^{k-1}$-competitive deterministic algorithm for the online $k$-taxi problem.
item.dc:creator: Christian Coester, Yichen Huang, Tze-Yang Poon

item.title: Combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication in $n^3 / 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.06717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For over fifty years, combinatorial algorithms for Boolean matrix multiplication (BMM) and triangle detection saved only polylogarithmic factors over cubic time. At STOC 2024, Abboud, Fischer, Kelley, Lovett, and Meka broke this barrier with a deterministic $O(n^3 / 2^{\Omega((\log n)^{1/7})})$-time algorithm, and asked whether $n^3 / 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ time is achievable. We answer this question in the affirmative, giving deterministic combinatorial algorithms for both BMM and triangle detection running in $O(n^3 / 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})})$ time. Following Abboud et al., we decompose $(A,B)$ into pairs of submatrices $(A_k,B_k)$, called \emph{pieces}, each of which is either sparse or pseudorandom in a sense that forces $A_k\star B_k$ to be nearly all-ones on its vertex sets. Whereas their decomposition produces $2^{O(d^7)}$ pieces at regularity parameter $d$, we obtain $2^{O(d^2)}$ pieces, directly improving the runtime exponent from $(\log n)^{1/7}$ to $\sqrt{\log n}$. Prior work found pseudorandom pieces by repeatedly restricting to denser submatrices, paying worst-case vertex losses at each step that compounded across nested recursion levels, together with an expensive derandomization step. We eliminate the extra powers of $d$ by matching the vertex loss at each step to the size of its density jump so losses telescope across scales, derandomizing witness search via $L_d$-norm estimation so the sampler length stays $2^{O(d)}$, and bounding overlap across the recursion with a fractional density-weighted volume budget rather than raw submatrix volume.
item.dc:creator: Piaoyang Cui, Yiming Liu, David P. Woodruff

item.title: Generalized Sorting via Four-Cycles
item.description: arXiv:2611.06745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the generalized sorting problem where only a subset of the pairs can be compared. Equivalently, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge graph $G=(V, E)$ where the vertex set $V$ is to be sorted, and the edge set $E$ indicates possible comparisons. The goal is to sort $V$ with as few (adaptive) queries to $E$ as possible. When $G$ is the complete graph, the problem is equivalent to standard sorting for which $\Theta(n \log n)$ queries are sufficient and necessary. All classical sorting algorithms crucially rely on the ability to compare any pair and do not imply an $o(n^2)$-query algorithm in the general case. This was improved 15 years ago by Huang, Kannan, and Khanna [FOCS'11] who achieved a bound of $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$. Kuszmaul and Narayanan [FOCS'21] later gave a bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{m n})$, which is more efficient for sparse graphs, but matches the $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for dense graphs. In this paper, we present an algorithm for generalized sorting that makes at most $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ queries, therefore breaking the longstanding $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for all graphs. The key to our result is to query edges that belong to many (specific types of) four-cycles. We show that querying such edges allows the algorithm to verify the direction of many other edges (specifically, their opposing edges in the four-cycles) and thus achieve a much better amortized query cost.
item.dc:creator: Soheil Behnezhad, Shane Ferrante

item.title: Approximation and Hardness for the Data Validation Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.06773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finnah, G\"onsch and Otto [Eur. J. Oper. Res. 2025] recently introduced the Data Validation Problem (DVP): Given a transitive directed acyclic graph $G$ on $n$ vertices (resp. tasks) and $m$ edges (resp. precedences) and a probing budget, a policy can successively pay a probing fee and probe an edge in $G$ as long as the total probing fees do not exceed the budget. If a probe succeeds, the targeted edge $e$ is removed from $G$ and we receive a reward; if the probe fails, the edge stays in $G$ and cannot be probed again. We seek a policy with maximum expected cumulative reward. Crucially, $G$ must stay transitive throughout the probing process, so a policy can only challenge the precedence between consecutive tasks, that is, only probe edges in the transitive reduction of the current precedence graph. We show that DVP is strongly NP-hard and W[1]-hard with the probing budget $T$ as a parameter, even in the deterministic case (when every probe has probability $0$ or $1$ to succeed) and with unit probing costs and rewards. For the same setting, we give an approximation-preserving reduction from the Densest $k$-Subgraph (D$k$S) Problem, with the consequence that there is no polynomial-time $2^{(\log n)^{1-\delta}}$-approximation algorithm and no FPT $\sqrt{T}$-approximation algorithm for DVP, assuming the Almost-Exponential Time Hypothesis and the Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis, respectively. We also present the first known policies with provable worst-case guarantees for DVP, namely an $m$-approximation algorithm for instances with uniform probabilities and probing costs, a $2T/p_{\min}^T$-approximation algorithm for general instances, where $p_{\min}$ is the minimum probing success probability, and an exact FPT algorithm on tournament graphs, in the deterministic setting.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Tinguely, G. Wessel van der Heijden

item.title: Finding full immersions is fixed-parameter tractable in labeled tour graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.06776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an $O_H(n^5)$-time algorithm to test whether an $n$-vertex labeled tour graph has a full immersion isomorphic to a labeled tour graph $H$. A labeled tour graph is a connected $4$-regular graph whose edges are labeled by binary vectors of fixed length. To obtain a full immersion, a vertex may be removed only by pairing up its four incident edges and "splitting off" both pairs, summing the labels within each pair. Even for one-bit labels, no polynomial-time algorithm was previously known for arbitrary fixed $H$. Our main tool is of independent interest: we give an algorithmic min-max theorem that, in particular, characterizes the maximum number of odd-length circuits in a rooted circuit decomposition of an Eulerian graph. Our results have implications for vertex-minors, whose study is motivated by applications in quantum networking, connections with graph minor theory, and the goal of developing an irrelevant vertex technique for dense graphs. For vertex-minors, circle graphs play the same role as planar graphs do for graph minors. As a corollary of our main theorem, we obtain a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for apex-vertex-minor testing in $k$-apex circle graphs. We also prove an irrelevant vertex theorem for such graphs of large rank-width. More broadly, our results are essential to forthcoming work of three of the authors proving a structure theorem for graphs with a forbidden vertex-minor. There, our min-max theorem plays the role of both the algorithmic $A$-paths and Two Paths Theorems.
item.dc:creator: Hadas Barabash, Jim Geelen, Rose McCarty, Caleb McFarland, Paul Wollan

item.title: The 3-Uniform Hyperclique Hypothesis is False
item.description: arXiv:2611.06813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present truly subquartic algorithms for detecting or counting 4-hypercliques in a 3-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices, disproving a popular hypothesis in fine-grained complexity. The result immediately implies a faster algorithm for finding a $k$-hyperclique in a 3-uniform hypergraph for all constant $k\ge 4$, and a faster exponential-time algorithm for Max-3-SAT.
item.dc:creator: Timothy M. Chan, Reina Itakura, Zhiyuan Ma, Yuancheng Yu

item.title: Deterministic Fault-Tolerant Connectivity Oracles with Subquadratic Space
item.description: arXiv:2611.06857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A fault-tolerant (FT) connectivity oracle for an $n$-vertex graph $G=(V,E)$ determines whether $G- F$ is connected for any query set $F\subseteq E$. When the number of failures is unrestricted, prior constructions exhibited a sharp contrast between randomization and determinism: randomized oracles use only $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space [Duan and Pettie, SICOMP 2020], whereas no deterministic construction was known to improve upon storing $G$ explicitly, requiring $\Theta(n^2)$ bits in the worst case. The promise that $F\subseteq E$ is essential for subquadratic space: allowing arbitrary queries $F\subseteq V\times V$ forces quadratic space. For queries containing at most $f$ failures, Khanna, Konrad, and Putterman [SODA 2027] recently constructed deterministic oracles using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{f}n)$ space that also report approximate distances with polylogarithmic stretch. Their result improves upon the classical $O(fn)$ space bound for deterministic connectivity oracles [P\u{a}tra\c{s}cu and Thorup, FOCS 2007], but offers no space savings over storing $G$ when $f=\Theta(n^2)$. We present the first deterministic connectivity oracles with subquadratic space for failure sets of unrestricted size, using $\widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})$ space. We also establish the first polynomial separation between deterministic and randomized connectivity oracles, proving that every deterministic oracle requires $\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{3/2})$ bits in the worst case. For queries containing at most $f$ failures, we obtain deterministic connectivity oracles using $\widetilde{O}(f^{2/5}n)$ space, improving the dependence on $f$ in the bound of Khanna et al., and prove a lower bound of $\widetilde{\Omega}(f^{1/4}n)$ bits.
item.dc:creator: Merav Parter, Elad Tzalik

item.title: Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations: A Strict Separation at $1-1/e$
item.description: arXiv:2611.06891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The matroid prophet-secretary problem asks an online algorithm to select an independent set of elements whose nonnegative values are drawn independently and revealed in uniformly random order. Its combinatorial-auction counterpart asks the algorithm to allocate disjoint bundles to arriving buyers with independently drawn XOS valuation functions. In both problems the distributions are known, and the benchmark is the expected offline optimum. Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give $(1-1/e)$-competitive algorithms for both settings. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits. For every matroid, we give a randomized $(1-1/e+\varepsilon_0)$-competitive algorithm, where $\varepsilon_0=10^{-6}$. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes $O(N^4)$ such queries in expectation and $O(N^4\log(N+2))$ in the worst case, where $N$ is the number of elements. For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that $1-1/e$ is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than $1-1/e$, even when the buyers' valuations are independent and identically distributed, every additive clause has coefficients in $\{0,1\}$, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.
item.dc:creator: Hossein Esfandiari, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi

item.title: Nonuniform Buy-at-Bulk Network Design: Improved Approximation and LP Integrality Gap
item.description: arXiv:2611.06894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design, we are given an undirected graph and $h$ terminal pairs with positive demands, and we must route every demand at minimum total cost when each network resource has two independent parameters: a fixed buying price paid once if the resource is used, and a per-unit rental cost (or physical length) paid proportionally to the traffic it carries. Unlike the uniform-cost or single-sink variants, the general multicommodity problem allows unrelated buying and rental metrics across arbitrary source--sink pairs, arbitrary demands, and both edge and node resources. We give a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$-approximation algorithm for undirected nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design. The guarantee holds for edge costs, node costs, and their combination, and applies to arbitrary positive rational demands with no dependence on the number of vertices or the numerical demand ratio. This improves upon the $O(\log^4 h)$ bound of Chekuri, Hajiaghayi, Kortsarz, and Salavatipour (2010) for unrestricted instances. Our result also establishes the same $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$ upper bound on the integrality gap of the natural affine multicommodity flow LP, bounding integral buying and rental costs separately against their fractional counterparts and preserving zero rental budgets exactly.
item.dc:creator: Iman Gholami, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi

item.title: Online Edge-Weighted Matching Beyond 0.55
item.description: arXiv:2611.06896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a $0.556195$-competitive randomized algorithm for edge-weighted online bipartite matching with free disposal, improving the $0.5368$ guarantee of Blanc and Charikar. The result holds for arbitrary nonnegative edge weights and any input sequence fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. Our algorithm builds on online correlated selection, introduced by Fahrbach, Huang, Tao, and Zadimoghaddam, and its multiway extension due to Blanc and Charikar. Our main contribution is a state-dependent primal--dual analysis of correlated selection. At each weight threshold, we track the state of the selection process jointly with an auxiliary failure event. The analysis accounts for arrivals below the threshold, which change the state without improving the matching value at that threshold. A potential function bounds the dual increase in both cases. We instantiate the analysis with an explicit win map that assigns a common score to an initial range of states. Its selection inequalities are verified by a finite computer-assisted proof covering every required candidate multiplicity and every real threshold; the verifiers are available in an accompanying repository. Triangular unit-weight inputs asymptotically attain the guarantee of the underlying ideal algorithm, proving that its analysis is tight.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Farhadi, Mohammad Hajiaghayi

item.title: A Simple Subquadratic Cut Query Protocol for Directed Reachability
item.description: arXiv:2611.06906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study $s$--$t$ reachability in an unweighted directed graph on $n$ vertices, accessed through a directed cut oracle: given $S\subseteq V$, the oracle returns the number of edges directed from $S$ to $V\setminus S$. Directed cut functions are submodular, and reachability asks whether the minimum $s$--$t$ cut has positive value. This connects the problem to the query complexity of submodular function minimisation. Whether or not reachability can be solved in truly subquadratic query complexity has been an outstanding open question for a decade. We give a simple algorithmic blueprint with two randomised implementations. The first uses $\widetilde O(n^{9/5})$ outgoing-cut queries; the second improves this bound to $\widetilde O(n^{5/3})$. The common idea is to construct an alternative orientation with the same underlying undirected graph and vertex-wise degree imbalances, thereby preserving reachability. We first approximate the target imbalances using an averaging and rounding procedure, then correct the remaining error with a flow. An earlier manuscript, made available in August 2026 in an online AI repository, reports an $\widetilde O(n^{3/2})$ query bound. Our contribution is a simple and comprehensible alternative approach that already achieves a polynomial saving over quadratic query complexity.
item.dc:creator: Henry Fleischmann, Sagnik Mukhopadhyay, Swagato Sanyal

item.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
item.description: arXiv:2611.05726v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying a chosen set of constraint families, and every candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, because a search that adds one family at a time then stops at the linear relaxation. The classical inequalities of lot sizing, network design and facility location rest on such zero-marginal groups. We prove that when each evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, any method that observes only bounds needs a covering number of evaluations, of order $k^w$, to find a hidden group of $w$ families, also on actual Dantzig-Wolfe relaxations. A prediction that misses $e$ members reduces the cost to $\Theta(k^e)$, through one staged search that does not need to know $e$, so the evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. We study two sources of predictions. A one-pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual is provably blind to groups whose families share no variable, and a language model reads the names and text of the model. JointDW verifies the prediction of the language model with the staged search and interleaves it with the lookahead at a bounded loss. Groups that strengthen the bound only jointly appear in a quarter of the MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved. There the strongest language models identify them about as often as the lookahead, their predictions rest on the names for textbook models, and reasoning about doubles the accuracy of the same model. On larger models with distracting families, the lookahead finds the group in one evaluation of three families. Language models given only the text seldom name it, while one reasoning model given every coefficient names it in all but one answer and then needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families.
item.dc:creator: Junbo Jacob Lian, Kaixuan Chen, Hanzhang Qin, Huiling Chen, Chaoyu Zhang, Chung-Piaw Teo

item.title: Sublinear Metric Distortion for Matching
item.description: arXiv:2611.05777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study metric distortion in one-sided matching. Given $n$ agents and $n$ items in an unknown metric space, our goal is to match agents to items so that the total distance between matched pairs is small. However, instead of direct access to the distances in the metric, we are only given each agent's ranking of the items by distance. What is the smallest worst-case approximation factor (called the distortion) that a mechanism can guarantee in expectation? Despite significant interest over the last decade, the best-known guarantee has been the $O(n)$ distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship since the beginning. We give a matching mechanism with distortion $O(n^{\log_4 3})$, the first sublinear upper bound. The key idea is to use a partial matching derived from a truncated version of either Random Serial Dictatorship or the Probabilistic Serial rule. We then complete this matching using a new, general-purpose cluster completion algorithm that ensures unmatched agents receive nearby items. Along the way, we pin down the optimal distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship and Probabilistic Serial up to logarithmic and constant factors, respectively, and give improved lower bounds for truthful mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Moses Charikar, Alireza Haqi, Jabari Hastings, Yichen Huang, Prasanna Ramakrishnan

item.title: Near linear mixing of random-cluster Glauber dynamics on random regular graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.05794v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the random-cluster model on locally treelike graphs at low temperatures. This is a model of dependent percolation parametrized by an edge probability $p \in (0,1)$ and a clustering weight $q \in [1,\infty)$, generalizing independent Bernoulli percolation ($q=1$) and closely related to the classical ferromagnetic Ising and Potts spin systems at integer $q$.
